turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. Um, I hope I'm not wasting your time with this, but... I guess I'm here because I've been having a little trouble lately. I'm in school for radiologic technology, which is great, I really like it. But... well, whenever I'm supposed to just sit still, like in the classroom or the radiology suite, I get this feeling like I'm completely crawling out of my skin. 

I know it probably sounds kind of silly for an 18-year-old to complain about sitting still, and I've really, really tried to just tough it out and be professional for months now. But I just can't seem to stop myself from shifting around constantly, or pacing, or, you know, finding some excuse to get up and move. I really want to do well in my program and not be a distraction to everyone else. Does that... does that make sense to come in for? I just want to make sure I'm doing the right thing by being here.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient reports constantly shifting around when expected to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions finding excuses to get up and move when they are supposed to be sitting still in the classroom or radiology suite.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling like they are 'crawling out of my skin' and pacing when expected to remain still.

turns.doctor_question: When did you first notice this feeling of not being able to sit still? Has this been something you've dealt with your whole life, or is it something that started more recently?
turns.patient_response:
Um, well... I guess it's actually been going on for a really long time. I hope it's okay if I go back a bit? But, um, my parents actually still talk about my elementary school parent-teacher conferences. 

I really don't want to sound like I was a troublemaker or a bad kid, I promise I wasn't trying to be disrespectful! But the teachers used to tell them that I was always out of my seat, or, you know, calling out in class, or rushing ahead to do assignments before they had even finished giving the directions. 

So... yeah, I guess that was happening way before middle school, even. It's definitely not just something that popped up recently since I started my radiology training. Is... is that the kind of information you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm answering your question right.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly recalls elementary school teachers stating they were 'always out of my seat.'
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms the doctor's question about the 'feeling of not being able to sit still,' noting it has been going on for a very long time.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient describes 'calling out in class' and rushing to start assignments before directions were fully given, demonstrating premature responses.

turns.doctor_question: Besides the difficulty sitting still and the restlessness, have you also noticed that you have trouble concentrating or staying focused on tasks, even when you're interested in them? turns.patient_response: Um, actually... no, not really. I mean, I hope it's okay to say that, but I don't think I have a problem with focusing. Like, when I'm studying for my radiology classes or listening to a lecture, my mind doesn't really wander off. I can follow what the instructors are saying just fine, and I keep track of everything. It's really just the... the physical part, the needing to move, that bothers me. I'm sorry if that's not what you were expecting me to say! I just want to be completely honest so I'm not wasting your time. Does that make sense?

turns.doctor_question: Besides school and your radiology training, have you noticed this restlessness and need to move affecting other areas of your life, like at home or in social situations? And has it caused problems for you in those settings?
turns.patient_response:
Um, well, at home it's not too bad, I guess. I can kind of just do my own thing and move around if I need to. But... um, it has been causing some, well, some issues in the clinical part of my training. 

I really don't want to sound like a bad student, because I promise I'm trying so, so hard to do everything right. But my clinical evaluations have kind of... taken a hit lately. The supervisors, they said that my... my behavior, like the shifting and the pacing, they said it disrupts the patient flow and makes teamwork harder for everyone else. 

They actually... um, they put me on a formal remediation plan. I feel awful about it, I really do. I'm just so worried that if I can't figure out how to just be normal and sit still, it could cost me my place in the whole program. And I really love this field, I want to be a good tech. Is it okay that I'm telling you all this? I just really want to fix it so I don't let anyone down anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms the doctor's question about restlessness, stating a need to 'move around' and describing 'pacing' that disrupts their work.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned earlier that in elementary school you would call out in class and rush ahead before instructions were finished. Do you still find yourself doing things impulsively like that—interrupting people, blurting things out, or acting without thinking things through first?
turns.patient_response:
Um, well... I guess I do still do that a little bit. I really try not to, because I know it's not polite, and I always feel so bad afterward. But sometimes... um, like when a supervisor is explaining a positioning step or, you know, asking me a question about a procedure, I'll just sort of jump in with the answer before they're even finished talking. 

I don't mean to be disrespectful or anything! I just get so eager to show them that I know the material, and then it just slips out. And then I realize I totally missed the second half of their sentence, which is usually the part that actually mattered. I always apologize right away when it happens. I really hope that doesn't make me sound like a terrible student... I am working on being better about waiting my turn to speak. Does that make sense, what I'm describing?

symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient notes she is 'working on being better about waiting my turn to speak,' indicating a difficulty with waiting her turn.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient describes interrupting supervisors while they are explaining steps or asking questions.
